passages.subtitle: How a road engineer made lighthouses visible from far out at sea

paragraphs.text: For most of history, the lights that warned sailors away from rocks and sandbanks were feeble things. The earliest lighthouses were simply towers with wood or coal fires burning on top, and later ones used candles or oil lamps enclosed in glass lanterns. In the 1780s the Swiss physicist Aimé Argand invented a lamp with a hollow, circular wick that drew air up through its centre. The Argand lamp burned far more brightly than earlier designs and produced less smoke, and it was quickly adopted by lighthouse authorities. To concentrate its light, engineers placed curved metal mirrors, known as reflectors, behind each lamp. Even so, the results were disappointing. A great deal of the light that struck a mirror was absorbed rather than reflected, and the polished metal tarnished quickly in the salty air of the coast, so keepers spent hours every day cleaning it.

The man who transformed lighthouses was not a sailor or a lamp-maker but a road engineer. Augustin Fresnel was born in Normandy in 1788. As a child he was such a slow learner that, according to his family, he could barely read at the age of eight, yet he later trained as an engineer and spent years building roads for the French government. His real passion, however, was light. In his spare time he carried out experiments that supported the theory that light travels as a wave. This was a controversial position at the time, since most scientists followed Isaac Newton in believing that light consisted of tiny particles. In 1819 Fresnel won a prize from the French Academy of Sciences for his work on diffraction, the way that light bends around obstacles, and his reputation was made.

In the same year he was appointed to France’s Lighthouse Commission, which had been asked to find a way of improving the country’s coastal lights. One obvious solution was to place a large glass lens in front of the lamp to focus its rays into a beam. The difficulty was that a lens big enough to collect most of the light would have to be extremely thick and heavy. Such a lens would absorb much of the light passing through it, and it was likely to crack while it was being made, because the thick glass cooled unevenly in the mould.

Fresnel’s solution rested on a simple observation: only the curved surfaces of a lens actually bend the light. The glass inside does nothing useful except add weight. He therefore divided the lens into a series of concentric rings, each of which was a thin slice of the curved surface of a much larger lens. Placed side by side, the rings bent the light just as a solid lens would, but the whole structure was a fraction of the thickness and could be built from separate pieces of glass. A similar idea had been suggested decades earlier by the French naturalist the Comte de Buffon, but Fresnel arrived at it independently and was the first to work out the mathematics needed to make it practical. Later designs, based on his calculations, added further rings of prisms above and below the centre. These caught the light escaping upwards and downwards from the lamp and reflected it into the beam, so that very little was wasted.

The first Fresnel lens was installed in 1823 in the Cordouan lighthouse, which stands on a rocky island at the mouth of the Gironde estuary in south-west France. Its light could be seen more than thirty kilometres out to sea, a dramatic improvement on the old reflectors. Because the lens was assembled from separate panels, it could also be made to rotate around the lamp, so that sailors saw the light as a series of flashes. By giving each lighthouse its own pattern of flashes, the authorities allowed sailors to identify exactly which lighthouse they were looking at, and therefore where they were.

Fresnel lenses were soon classified by size into what were called ‘orders’. The largest, the first-order lenses, were intended for major lights on dangerous coasts and could stand almost four metres tall. At the other end of the scale, sixth-order lenses were small enough to be carried by one person and were generally used to mark harbours and piers, where ships approached slowly and a long-range light was unnecessary.

Other countries were slower to adopt the new technology, partly because of its cost. In the United States, reflectors remained in use until a Lighthouse Board was created in 1852; within a decade almost every American lighthouse had been fitted with a Fresnel lens. Fresnel himself did not live to see his invention spread around the world. He suffered from poor health for most of his life and died of tuberculosis in 1827, at the age of thirty-nine. Today most lighthouses have been automated, and many of the great glass lenses have been replaced by electric lights and moved to museums. Yet Fresnel’s principle is all around us: it can be found in car headlights, in traffic signals, in solar power collectors and in the thin plastic magnifying sheets sold for reading small print.

passages.subtitle: The science behind adolescent sleep, and what schools are doing about it

paragraphs.text: Few sights are more familiar to parents than a teenager who stays up until after midnight and then cannot be woken for school the next morning. The behaviour is often put down to laziness, late-night screen use or simple rebellion. Over the past fifty years, however, sleep scientists have built up a very different explanation. Much of the problem, they argue, lies not in teenagers’ characters but in their biology.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The timing of sleep is controlled by two separate systems. The first is sleep pressure: from the moment we wake, a chemical called adenosine gradually builds up in the brain, and the longer we stay awake, the stronger the urge to sleep becomes. The second is the body’s internal clock, a small group of cells in the brain that keeps a roughly twenty-four-hour rhythm and signals the approach of night by triggering the release of the hormone melatonin. During puberty, both systems change. Melatonin is released later in the evening, in some cases up to two hours later than in younger children, and sleep pressure builds more slowly, so that teenagers can stay awake late without feeling tired.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Some of the earliest evidence came from summer ‘sleep camps’ run at Stanford University in the 1970s, where the researcher Mary Carskadon and her colleagues monitored children who stayed in the laboratory for several days at a time. The team expected to find that young people needed less sleep as they grew older. Instead, they found that when they were given the opportunity, adolescents slept about nine hours a night, and that this need did not fall as they passed through puberty. Older teenagers, in fact, became sleepier during the day. Years later, by measuring melatonin in saliva samples, Carskadon was able to show that the internal clock itself shifts later during adolescence.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The German researcher Till Roenneberg approached the question differently. Rather than studying small groups in a laboratory, he designed a questionnaire asking people when they went to sleep and woke up on days when they had no work or school. Analysing the replies of tens of thousands of people, he found that sleep timing becomes steadily later throughout adolescence, reaches its latest point at around the age of twenty, and then gradually becomes earlier again for the rest of life. The turning point is so consistent, Roenneberg suggested, that it could be used as a biological marker of the end of adolescence.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The trouble is that society does not run on teenage time. Many secondary schools start classes before eight o’clock, so students whose bodies are not ready to sleep until midnight are forced to wake long before they have had enough rest. During the week they build up a sleep debt, which they then try to repay by sleeping late at weekends, a pattern Roenneberg called ‘social jet lag’. Lack of sleep has been linked to poor concentration and memory, to low mood and depression, and to a higher risk of road accidents among young drivers.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: If the problem is caused by early starts, one solution is obvious: start school later. In the late 1990s, Kyla Wahlstrom of the University of Minnesota studied schools in the state that had moved their opening times from around half past seven to after eight. Students at these schools reported feeling more alert in class and showed fewer symptoms of depression, and attendance improved. More recently, a team from the University of Washington led by Horacio de la Iglesia studied the effect of a change in Seattle, where in 2016 the start of the high-school day was moved from 7.50 to 8.45. Rather than relying on what students said, the researchers asked them to wear wrist monitors that recorded their activity day and night. The monitors showed that students slept an extra thirty-four minutes on school nights, and their grades in the biology course the researchers followed rose by more than four per cent.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Changing school hours is not as simple as it sounds. School districts often share buses between primary and secondary schools, so moving one timetable means moving the other. Later finishing times can also clash with after-school sports, part-time jobs and parents’ working hours. Nevertheless, opinion is shifting. In 2014 the American Academy of Pediatrics recommended that middle and high schools should not start before 8.30 a.m., and in 2019 California became the first American state to make this a legal requirement. In the meantime, experts advise teenagers to keep regular hours and to avoid bright screens late in the evening, which can delay the internal clock still further.
paragraphs.label: G

passages.subtitle: The promise and the problems of de-extinction

paragraphs.text: Few scientific ideas have captured the public imagination as quickly as ‘de-extinction’, the project of bringing vanished species back to life. The idea owes much of its appeal to films such as Jurassic Park, and it has attracted generous funding from investors. One American company, founded in 2021, has announced plans to recreate the woolly mammoth, the dodo and the thylacine, or Tasmanian tiger. Yet behind the headlines lie difficult questions, not only about whether such projects can succeed but about whether they should be attempted at all.

The first, and so far only, animal to be brought back from extinction in the strict sense was a Pyrenean ibex, a wild goat from the mountains between France and Spain. The last member of the species, a female named Celia, died in 2000, but scientists had already taken and frozen samples of her skin cells. In 2003 they used these cells to create a clone, which was carried by a goat acting as a surrogate mother. The kid was born alive but died within minutes because of a defect in its lungs. The experiment is often described as a failure, but it would be wrong to see it only in those terms: it proved, for the first time, that an extinct animal could be born again, even if only briefly.

Cloning, however, requires living cells, and these do not exist for species that died out long ago. For the mammoth, which disappeared around four thousand years ago, scientists instead propose to edit the DNA of its closest living relative, the Asian elephant, adding genes for features such as thick hair and a layer of fat that would help the animal survive in the cold. In 2025 the same company announced that it had produced three wolf pups whose DNA had been altered to give them some of the characteristics of the dire wolf, a much larger animal that became extinct more than ten thousand years ago. The announcement made headlines around the world, but many biologists objected to the claim that the dire wolf had been ‘brought back’. In my view they were right to do so. An elephant with a hairy coat is not a mammoth; it is an elephant hybrid designed to resemble one. We should be honest about what the technology can and cannot do.

Supporters of mammoth de-extinction argue that the animals would bring environmental benefits. In the Arctic, the ground beneath the surface is frozen all year round. This permafrost contains vast quantities of carbon, which would be released into the atmosphere if it thawed. Some scientists believe that large herds of plant-eating animals could help to keep the permafrost frozen by trampling down the snow, which otherwise acts like a blanket that keeps the ground beneath it warm, and by turning shrubland back into grassland. It is an intriguing argument, but it depends on releasing very large numbers of animals, and an elephant pregnancy lasts almost two years. Even if everything went to plan, it would take many decades to produce a herd large enough to make any difference.

There are also serious ethical concerns. The Asian elephant is itself an endangered species, and any programme to produce mammoth-like animals would require elephants to act as surrogate mothers, perhaps repeatedly. Elephants are intelligent, social animals, and I find it hard to see how this could be justified. Researchers have suggested that an artificial womb might one day solve the problem, but no such device yet exists for an animal of this size.

A further worry is what economists call ‘moral hazard’: the danger that people behave less carefully when they believe they are protected from the consequences of their actions. If the public comes to believe that extinction can be reversed, it may feel less urgency about protecting species that are still alive. Moreover, the money spent on de-extinction is money that is not available for conservation. Every year, wildlife organisations are forced to choose which threatened species to save because they lack the funding to save them all.

None of this means that the science behind de-extinction is worthless. In 2020 American scientists produced a black-footed ferret named Elizabeth Ann from the cells of a ferret that had died in 1988. The black-footed ferret is one of the rarest mammals in North America, and all the surviving animals are descended from just a handful of individuals, which makes them vulnerable to disease. Because the cells came from an animal with no living descendants, the clone could add new genetic variety to the population. It is in cases like this, helping endangered species to survive rather than recreating lost ones, that the strongest case for the technology lies. The mammoth may make the headlines, but the ferret is the real success story.
